section_summary: This section documents mounting American public and official debate over exports of scrap iron, petroleum, aircraft, cotton, metals, machinery, and other strategically useful materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. It contains citizen and missionary appeals for an embargo, State Department explanations of existing neutrality and arms-export law, statistical studies of Japanese dependence on foreign supplies, and diplomatic discussions with Britain and France about restricting iron and ore shipments. The closing documents concern Senator Key Pittman’s proposed legislation authorizing trade restrictions against violators of the Nine-Power Treaty.

subfiles.title: Baker urges an end to American war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Baker forwards a published letter and urges the United States to stop supplying Japan with iron, steel, and other war materials.
subfiles.summary: Baker argues American exports strengthen Japan for eventual conflict with the US and that economic action could halt Japan without war.

subfiles.title: Japan Viewed as an Enemy Whom We Are Arming
subfiles.about: A published letter argues that American materials support Japanese naval expansion and threaten future U.S. security.
subfiles.summary: Clipping 'Japan Viewed as an Enemy Whom We Are Arming': Japanese naval plans prompt British and American building; calls for ending exports strengthening Japan.

subfiles.title: Welles replies to Baker on exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: Welles acknowledges Baker’s views and sends a Department statement on current exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles thanks Baker for his March 23 letter on iron, steel and war materials and encloses the Department's statement.

subfiles.title: Routing note for file 894.24/635
subfiles.about: A brief administrative slip directs the file numbered 894.24/635 back to A/H.
subfiles.summary: Routing note for file 894.24/635 on the composition of exported scrap.

subfiles.title: Character of Scrap Exported in 1937
subfiles.about: The memorandum classifies 1937 American scrap exports by grade and estimates how much could have been used domestically.
subfiles.summary: Of 4,039,143 tons of scrap exported in 1937, about 54 percent might otherwise have served American mills; the remaining 46 percent was low-value material with little domestic demand.

subfiles.title: Some Pro and Con Considerations with Respect to the Proposed Restriction of Exports of Scrap Iron and Steel
subfiles.about: The memorandum weighs strategic arguments for restricting scrap exports against economic, diplomatic, and practical objections.
subfiles.summary: The case for restriction rests on rapidly growing exports to Japan, Italy, and Germany and their usefulness to armaments industries. The objections emphasize Japan’s ability to substitute pig iron, ore, and semi-manufactured products, and argue that effective pressure would also require controls on petroleum, copper, nickel, and other supplies. The memorandum also warns of discrimination against the scrap trade, retaliation, conflicts with American commercial policy, and demands for wider protectionism.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 100 on George A. Fitch’s criticism of American war-material sales
subfiles.about: Peck reports George A. Fitch’s broadcasts and letter condemning American material support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Peck encloses a newspaper item containing Fitch’s appeal to President Roosevelt. He agrees that Japanese bombing of undefended Chinese cities deserves condemnation but fears Fitch’s rhetoric may inflame or mislead Chinese opinion about the actual position of the American government and people.

subfiles.title: Roosevelt Asked to Stop War Supply to Japan
subfiles.about: Fitch appeals to Roosevelt to end sales of gasoline, oil, scrap iron, and other materials used by Japan in China.
subfiles.summary: Fitch describes civilian deaths and destruction from Japanese bombing at Guiyang, Wanxian and Xi'an, calling continued American supply of strategic materials complicity and a future danger, and asks decisive action.

subfiles.title: Davison reports a rumor of mustard-gas exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Davison reports an unverified allegation that a Pacific Coast refinery was producing mustard gas for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Davison reports a rumor that a refinery, presumed Shell, might make mustard gas from ethylene, and asks the Department to investigate.

subfiles.title: State Department response concerning alleged mustard-gas exports
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that mustard gas requires an export license and that none has been sought or issued for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost sends the arms-traffic pamphlet, noting mustard gas is in the President's list of implements of war and no export licenses for Japan were requested or granted; asks for corroboration.

subfiles.title: American Committee forwards photographs of American aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Norton sends two sets of photographs concerning American assistance to Japan at Harry B. Price’s request.
subfiles.summary: The American Committee tells Hornbeck photographs of American aid to Japan are being sent separately.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of the photographs
subfiles.about: Hornbeck thanks Price for arranging delivery of two sets of photographs.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck confirms the pictures mentioned in Norton's March 16 letter arrived.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to the Chengdu American Community neutrality message
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to a telegram reporting the Chengdu American Community’s views on pending neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to the Chengdu American Community message opposing equal treatment of Japan and China and urging an end to aid to Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 251 transmitting the Chengdu American Community appeal
subfiles.about: Peck transmits an urgent appeal from Americans in Chengdu concerning pending U.S. neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 251: the Chengdu American Community opposes equal-treatment legislation and asks America to end military and economic aid to Japan.

subfiles.title: Utilization by Japan of Cotton
subfiles.about: The memorandum estimates how much imported cotton could have been available for Japanese military use and supplies detailed trade and mill-consumption tables.
subfiles.summary: Department of Agriculture data show that most imported cotton entered mills belonging to the Japan Cotton Spinners Association and that a substantial share was re-exported as manufactured goods. The memorandum estimates that no more than 49 percent of imports in 1936–1937, and no more than 43 percent during the first eleven months of 1938, could have served military purposes. Attached tables cover imports, exports, mill consumption, growths of cotton, and yarn supply and distribution.

subfiles.title: Senator Davis forwards Beiler’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Davis asks Hull to review Irwin R. Beiler’s enclosed letter and provide information for a response.
subfiles.summary: Senator Davis forwards constituent Beiler's inquiry and asks that the enclosure be returned with the information.

subfiles.title: Beiler calls for a complete embargo on aggressor nations
subfiles.about: Beiler protests reported airplane shipments to Japan and advocates a comprehensive embargo on war materials.
subfiles.summary: Beiler says American trade makes the US an abettor of Japanese aggression, rejects cash-and-carry and says public sentiment favors a complete embargo on aggressors.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Davis on aircraft and arms exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Hull provides official reports and explains current policy concerning arms and aeronautical exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses the Munitions Board report and statements; aircraft makers fully comply, no new licenses for arms or aircraft to Japan were sought or issued in three months, and older shipments should cease.

subfiles.title: Glover appeals for an end to war-material supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Glover draws on his missionary experience in China to urge prompt termination of American material support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Glover, recently in China, describes devastation and argues American strategic exports make the US a partner in aggression; he believes cutting supplies would reduce war risk.

subfiles.title: Department response to Robert Hall Glover
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Glover’s appeal and outlines its policy on aeronautical and arms exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Department encloses its statement, recalls disapproval of supplying aircraft to forces bombing civilians, and says no new Japan arms licenses in three months, with older shipments ending soon.

subfiles.title: Scrap Iron
subfiles.about: The editorial condemns simultaneous American shipments of scrap iron to Japan and humanitarian aid to wounded Chinese.
subfiles.summary: Editorial contrasts bandages for Chinese casualties with ships loading scrap for Japan, claiming Roosevelt could invoke the neutrality law and embargo scrap iron without new legislation.

subfiles.title: Yost corrects the News-Tribune’s interpretation of the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains that existing neutrality legislation does not authorize an embargo on scrap iron or comparable raw materials.
subfiles.summary: Yost corrects the News-Tribune: under Section 1(d) of the 1937 Act and the proclamation, scrap iron is excluded, so new legislation would be required.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hamilton’s conversation with Representative Keller
subfiles.about: The sheet references a memorandum about Representative Keller’s contemplated resolution embargoing oil, scrap iron, and other commodities to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Hamilton's conversation with Representative Keller, who was considering legislation to ban selected commodity exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Fitch’s March 13 radio broadcast
subfiles.about: The sheet references Peck’s telegram reporting George A. Fitch’s broadcast against American support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Fitch's March 13 broadcast urging prohibition of materials essential to Japan's war machine.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 176 reporting Fitch’s radio broadcast
subfiles.about: Peck transmits extensive excerpts from George A. Fitch’s broadcast urging Americans to halt strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 176: Fitch argues high-test gasoline, scrap iron and copper sales enable Japanese bombing of Chinese cities, calls trade a partnership in crimes and urges pressure on Congress.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to rumored Japanese purchase of American motor trucks
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a memorandum concerning a rumored large purchase of American trucks by Japanese interests in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Hamilton's talk with a General Motors representative about rumored Japanese purchase of American trucks possibly supporting Manchuria activity.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese pressure on Dodge and Seymour
subfiles.about: The sheet references Ambassador Grew’s telegram concerning pressure on an American corporation to transfer profits to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Dodge and Seymour reportedly profited from American manufactures in Japanese munitions production; Grew asks whether to make representations.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 162 on pressure against Dodge and Seymour
subfiles.about: Grew reports Japanese official pressure on Dodge and Seymour to transfer profits from munitions-related sales into Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 162: the embassy thinks the commodities warrant Department review and advised the company to present its case in Washington.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to French and British iron supplies for Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet summarizes Bullitt’s report on French Indochinese and British iron supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: France stopped Indochina iron deliveries but Japan compensated from British possessions; Leger saw colonial restrictions of limited value while the US supplies; possible French-British-American coordination.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Victor Mallet
subfiles.about: Moffat discourages a prospective British request for joint action to restrict iron supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mallet: France stopped Indochina iron after the Spratly seizure but Japan found supplies in Malaya and the US; Moffat says the US acts independently and a British approach could complicate Pittman's legislation.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction to the Ambassador in Paris
subfiles.about: The Secretary forwards the April 19 Mallet-Moffat memorandum concerning iron shipments from French Indochina to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Confidential instruction sends the Paris ambassador the memorandum on the Department's effort to avert a British proposal for coordinated restrictions.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction No. 682 to the Ambassador in London
subfiles.about: The Secretary confidentially sends the April 19 memorandum on iron shipments from French Indochina to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Confidential Instruction No. 682 gives London the record of Moffat's conversation with the British counselor on British and French action over Japanese iron access.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction to the Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Secretary transmits the April 19 memorandum concerning French Indochinese iron shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo receives the memorandum explaining the Department's concern about being approached for coordinated embargo action.

subfiles.title: Follow-up memorandum on Mallet’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Moffat reports that Britain has discouraged a French proposal for a joint embargo approach to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Mallet clarifies France was concerned with ores, not scrap; Britain discouraged a joint approach to Washington, and he expects nothing further.

subfiles.title: Confidential follow-up instruction No. 691 to London
subfiles.about: The Secretary forwards Moffat’s April 29 follow-up memorandum concerning iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 691 tells London Britain discouraged the proposed joint approach to the US.

subfiles.title: Confidential follow-up instruction No. 1466 to Paris
subfiles.about: The Secretary forwards the April 29 Mallet-Moffat memorandum to the Paris embassy.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 1466 tells Paris Britain blocked the joint British-French approach to Washington.

subfiles.title: Confidential follow-up instruction No. 1722 to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Secretary sends the Tokyo embassy Moffat’s April 29 memorandum on the abandoned embargo approach.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 1722 tells Tokyo the British discouraged France's plan to approach the US jointly on Indochinese iron.

subfiles.title: Welles asks Hornbeck how to answer the Greater Boston Committee
subfiles.about: Welles requests a proposed reply to a committee seeking a public message for an anti-Japan rally.
subfiles.summary: Welles doubts he can send the endorsement the Greater Boston Committee requests and asks Hornbeck what response to make.

subfiles.title: Greater Boston Committee requests a message from Welles
subfiles.about: The committee asks Welles to send a letter or telegram for an April 22 rally advocating an end to shipments useful to Japan’s war effort.
subfiles.summary: Greater Boston Committee asks Welles for a message to be read at an Old South Meeting House meeting on a resolution to stop war materials reaching Japan.

subfiles.title: Stop Arming Japan rally announcement
subfiles.from: Greater Boston Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The flyer advertises an April 22 rally against American participation in Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Stop Arming Japan rally flyer: speakers Freda Utley and Dominick Gavin, chairman Courtenay Crocker, within a nationwide campaign week of April 16-23.

subfiles.title: Welles declines to provide a message for the Boston rally
subfiles.about: Welles declines the committee’s request because neutrality policy and related resolutions were under congressional consideration.
subfiles.summary: Welles notes that the President had raised neutrality legislation in his January 4 message and that Senate and House committees were holding hearings. Because the rally’s subject overlapped with matters pending before Congress, he says a statement for public reading would be inappropriate.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to mahogany blocks for rifle stocks
subfiles.about: The sheet references a Honduras despatch concerning Roy B. Nutter’s offer to sell mahogany blocks for rifle stocks.
subfiles.summary: The record identifies the commodity as mahogany suitable for firearms manufacture. It directs readers to Despatch No. 657 from Honduras.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 657 on mahogany blocks for rifle stocks
subfiles.from: Fred K. Salter, for the Minister in Honduras
subfiles.about: The legation reports Roy B. Nutter’s attempt to market Honduran mahogany blocks for rifle stocks in the United States or Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 657: Nutter could cut 250,000 rifle-stock mahogany blocks within six weeks; after a Japanese market suggestion he offered them at 25 cents each and got no response; legation advised contacting Springfield Armory.

subfiles.title: Quantities and values of selected American exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State, using Department of Commerce data
subfiles.about: The table compares quantities and values of selected exports to Japan in 1937, 1938, and the first two months of 1938 and 1939.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion includes power-driven metalworking machinery and automobiles, parts, and accessories. A note states that the figures were compiled from Department of Commerce data.

subfiles.title: Percentage of Certain Materials Exported from the United States to Japan in 1938
subfiles.about: The table measures Japan’s share of total American exports of strategically important commodities in 1938.
subfiles.summary: 1938 table: Japan received large shares of US pig iron (68.5 percent), specified steel (56.3 percent), scrap (49 percent), copper, cotton, petroleum and machinery.

subfiles.title: Imports of Certain Materials into Japan in 1936 and 1937
subfiles.about: The table compares Japanese imports from the United States with other actual and potential foreign sources.
subfiles.summary: Table of Japan's 1936-1937 imports, with the US supplying high shares of copper and automobiles and alternative sources worldwide.

subfiles.title: Welles asks Hamilton to draft a reply
subfiles.about: Welles requests an appropriate draft response for his signature.
subfiles.summary: Welles asks Hamilton to draft a reply, concerning Charles Whiting Baker's renewed advocacy of trade restrictions on Japan.

subfiles.title: Baker forwards his letter to Senator Pittman
subfiles.about: Baker sends Welles a copy of his appeal to Senator Pittman for strong restrictions on trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Baker forwards his letter to Senator Pittman, expected to introduce legislation curbing Japanese trade, proposing prohibitive tariffs to avoid Neutrality Act complications.

subfiles.title: Baker urges Pittman to curb trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Baker urges Pittman to enact sweeping restrictions on exports to and imports from Japan as a measure of American self-defense.
subfiles.summary: Baker urges Pittman to curb trade with Japan, claiming ending strategic exports would protect American security better than battleships and that China's resistance offers a temporary opportunity.

subfiles.title: Welles acknowledges Baker’s letter on the Pittman bill
subfiles.about: Welles acknowledges Baker’s letter and the enclosed copy of his communication to Senator Pittman.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges Baker's letter on the Pittman bill, read with interest.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Tokyo on Pittman’s Nine-Power Treaty bill
subfiles.about: The Department urgently reports Pittman’s introduction of a bill authorizing trade restrictions against violators of the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Telegram to Tokyo quotes Pittman saying he drafted the Nine-Power Treaty bill alone, and Hull saying he first learned of it from the news.

subfiles.title: Press bulletins on Pittman’s neutrality and trade-restriction bill
subfiles.about: A series of wire bulletins describes Pittman’s proposal to empower the President to restrict commerce with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Press bulletins: Pittman's bill would allow presidential restrictions against a violator of the Nine-Power Treaty, limited to protecting American lives and rights after diplomatic efforts; Pittman says it was his own proposal.
